meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Holding on to anger is like grasping a hot coal with the intent of throwing it at someone else; you are the one who gets burned'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha. The metaphor traces to Buddhaghosa's 5th-century Visuddhimagga; the popular wording is a modern paraphrase from a 1987 book.

answer.label: Not Gautama Buddha — a paraphrase of Buddhaghosa
answer.authorDates: fl. 5th century CE · Theravada Buddhist commentator
answer.sourceLine: The hot-coal image is genuinely Buddhist, but it comes from the scholar-monk Buddhaghosa, not the Buddha himself. It appears in his 5th-century commentary the Visuddhimagga (“The Path of Purification”) — not in the Buddha’s own recorded discourses — and the familiar English wording is a modern paraphrase that spread from a 1987 self-help book, as documented by Quote Investigator.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Pe Maung Tin, The Path of Purity (1931)
Part II, ch. IX (The Developing of Love)

source.excerpt: … like a man who seizes with both hands glowing live coals or dung in order to strike another man therewith, but who first burns and befouls himself.
trail: 5th century CE — the metaphor is written by Buddhaghosa in the Visuddhimagga, an interpretive commentary, as traced by Quote Investigator.
1931 — Pe Maung Tin’s English translation renders it “glowing live coals or dung … who first burns and befouls himself,” per QI’s citation.
1987–88 — Joan Borysenko’s Minding the Body, Mending the Mind puts the simile in the Buddha’s mouth, seeding the modern wording (QI).
Verdict — Fake Buddha Quotes confirms it is not canonical and never appears in the Buddha’s recorded words.
source.excerptNote: From Pe Maung Tin’s 1931 translation of the Visuddhimagga. The original couples the coal with dung/excrement and describes a person acting on anger — not “holding on to” it. The popular quote drops the dung, adds the “holding on” framing, and reads as first-person advice.
source.rightsNote: The underlying metaphor is Buddhaghosa’s 5th-century Visuddhimagga, whose Pali original is long in the public domain. But the exact popular English wording is a modern paraphrase with no single identifiable author — it diverges from every documented translation, including Pe Maung Tin’s 1931 rendering — so no clear copyright status can be asserted for this specific phrasing.

author.name: Buddhaghosa
author.heading: About Buddhaghosa
author.metaLine: fl. 5th century CE · Theravada Buddhist scholar-monk · author of the Visuddhimagga
author.bio: Buddhaghosa was a 5th-century Indian Theravada commentator who worked at the Mahavihara in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka. His masterwork, the Visuddhimagga (“The Path of Purification”), systematizes Theravada doctrine and meditation, and it is there — not in the Buddha’s own sermons — that the vivid image of seizing a live coal to strike another appears. His writings shaped Theravada thought for centuries, but they are interpretive commentary written roughly a millennium after the Buddha’s death.

misattribution.heading: A genuine Buddhist image, wrongly signed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet's most reshared “Buddha” lines — and it is not his. The thought is authentically Buddhist, but the words are a modern paraphrase of a later commentator.

items.why: The Buddha never said this. The metaphor was written roughly a thousand years after his death by the commentator Buddhaghosa in the Visuddhimagga, per Quote Investigator.

The original describes a person acting on anger by seizing “glowing live coals or dung” and burning himself first. The popular version drops the dung, reframes it as “holding on to” anger, and adds the throwing image — a paraphrase, not a translation (Fake Buddha Quotes).
Her book Minding the Body, Mending the Mind placed the simile directly in the Buddha’s mouth, and the modern wording spread from there (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Buddhaghosa, a 5th-century commentator — and even his words describe acting on anger, not the tidy “hot coal you throw” aphorism people now quote (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is genuinely rooted in Buddhist thought, which is why it feels so plausible as a Buddha quote — and that plausibility is exactly what let the misattribution spread. The image of harming yourself by clutching a burning coal really does appear in the Theravada tradition; it just belongs to a 5th-century commentary, not to the historical Buddha’s discourses.

The gap between Buddhaghosa’s original and the viral version is instructive: the source warns against acting on anger (striking someone), while the popular saying is about holding on to it. The paraphrase is arguably wiser than the original — but it is not what anyone in the canon actually said.
context.pull: Authentically Buddhist in spirit — but written by a commentator, not the Buddha, and reworded by the modern self-help shelf.
